title: How Russia Is Attacking the Midterms with a Mother Jones Deepfake

reading.body:
This is an impersonation failure rather than a model error in the ordinary sense. A synthetic video was made to look like reporting from an established news outlet, and it asserted specific false claims as fact, including a payment figure, a broadcast count, and a set of stolen emails. The fabrication did not need to be convincing to specialists, only to travel as though it carried a newsroom's authority.

The failure sits at the distribution layer. The video spread through posts on X, and the platform removed the reported posts only after the outlet it impersonated complained, and then under its trademark policy rather than on the basis of the content being false. Catching it earlier would have required the platform to verify the provenance of media branded as a major outlet, or to detect synthetic video at upload, before the posts accumulated their views. Nothing in the reporting indicates that any such check existed.

What is not established is the operation's authorship and intent. The attribution to a named Russian network and the claim that the effort was meant to influence the midterms come from researchers and from the outlet's own account, not from a finding by any authority.

reports.title: How Russia Is Attacking the Midterms with a Mother Jones Deepfake

summary:
A Russian disinformation network called Storm-1679 or Matryoshka spread a fake video branded as Mother Jones. It falsely claimed the Democratic National Committee paid $259 million to CNN head Mark Thompson to promote gender transition among children. It also said CNN aired 8,970 such reports and cited emails supposedly stolen by Anonymous. An X account posted it, drawing 155,000 views, while another account got 50,000. The video was fake and part of a Russian effort to influence the 2026 midterms and help Donald Trump and the GOP.

Researchers at @antibot4navalny identified the operation. The network has also used fake celebrity videos and false reports about Democratic candidates, often made to look like they came from major US media outlets. After Mother Jones complained, X removed the reported posts for violating its trademark policy. The article says the current campaign has not yet achieved great reach, but it may continue. It notes that the Trump administration closed FBI, intelligence, and State Department units that tracked foreign disinformation, leaving the US less able to defend against Russian influence in the midterms.
